blocks.prompt: Eight Worlds Around One Star
blocks.text: Our Sun is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas. It is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Eight planets travel around the Sun. The four closest ones are made of rock. Earth is one of those. The four far ones are giants made mostly of gas and ice. Jupiter is the biggest of all. Nothing pushes the planets along. They just keep going. The Sun pulls on them, and that pull bends their path into a loop. We call one trip around the Sun a year.

3.title: Eight Worlds Around One Star

blocks.prompt: Why the Planets Never Stop
blocks.text:
Look up at night and the sky seems still. It is not. Everything up there is moving, and the Sun is the reason.

Our solar system is one star plus everything caught in its pull. Eight planets circle the Sun. The four nearest are small and rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. Then comes a wide gap holding millions of chunks of rock, called the asteroid belt. Past the gap sit the four giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Jupiter alone is heavier than all the other planets put together.

Nothing pushes the planets. In space there is almost nothing to slow them down, so they keep the speed they started with. Gravity from the Sun tugs them sideways, and that steady tug bends a straight path into a loop. The planets are falling toward the Sun and missing it, over and over, forever.

The closer a planet sits, the faster it has to move. Mercury finishes a lap in 88 days. Neptune needs 165 Earth years. Nobody born on Neptune would live long enough to have a first birthday.

blocks.prompt: How to Build a Solar System
blocks.text:
Four and a half billion years ago there were no planets here. There was a cloud of gas and dust, drifting between the stars, cold and shapeless. Something disturbed it. The cloud began to collapse under its own gravity, and as it fell inward it spun, the way a skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms. The spin flattened the cloud into a disk with a hot lump at the middle. That lump became the Sun, and it took almost everything: 99.8 percent of all the material in the cloud.

The planets are built from the 0.2 percent left over. Grains of dust in the disk bumped into each other and stuck, making pebbles, then boulders, then rocks the size of cities. The big ones swept up the small ones.

Where you ended up depended on where you formed. Close to the young Sun it was far too hot for ice to survive, so only metal and rock stayed solid. There was not much of it, so the planets built there stayed small: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars. Farther out, past a boundary astronomers call the frost line, water froze into countless grains of ice. Suddenly there was much more solid material to work with. Cores grew huge, and once a core was heavy enough, its gravity grabbed hydrogen and helium straight out of the disk. Jupiter and Saturn ballooned. Uranus and Neptune, forming later and farther out, grabbed less.

Then the young Sun blew the leftover gas away, and building stopped. What remains is what you see: rock near the fire, giants in the cold, and rubble in the gaps that never finished becoming anything.

5.title: Eight Worlds Around One Star
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Neptune orbits 30 times farther out than Earth
Sunlight reaches Earth in 8 minutes, Neptune in 4 hours
The Kuiper Belt lies beyond Neptune
Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012
The Oort Cloud may reach 100,000 times the Earth to Sun distance
No telescope has ever seen an Oort Cloud object in place

blocks.prompt: Where Does the Solar System End?
blocks.text:
Ask where the solar system stops and you will get at least three answers, all of them defensible.

The first answer is Neptune. It is the last of the eight planets, thirty times farther from the Sun than Earth is. Sunlight takes eight minutes to reach us and about four hours to reach Neptune. That is a tidy edge, and it is also wrong, because a great deal of solar system lies past it.

The second answer is the Kuiper Belt, a broad ring of frozen bodies beyond Neptune's orbit. Pluto lives there, and so do more than a hundred thousand objects wider than a hundred kilometers, leftovers from the disk that never assembled into a planet. The comets that return every few decades come from this region.

The third answer belongs to the Sun rather than to any object. The Sun does not only shine, it leaks. A thin wind of charged particles streams outward in every direction at hundreds of kilometers per second, carving a bubble in the gas that drifts between the stars. That bubble is the heliosphere, and its wall is the heliopause: the place where the solar wind finally loses its push and interstellar space takes over. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, crossed that wall in August 2012 and became the first human object in interstellar space. By that measure the solar system has a real edge, and we have already left it.

And yet the Sun's gravity does not stop at the heliopause. It reaches on, thinning but never quite failing, for something like a hundred thousand times the distance from here to the Sun. Out there, astronomers think, sits the Oort Cloud: a vast shell of icy bodies so distant and so faint that nobody has ever seen one in place. We infer it from the long comets that fall inward from every direction of the sky, which is exactly what you would expect from a shell rather than a ring. If the Oort Cloud is the border, then Voyager 1, moving at seventeen kilometers per second, needs roughly three hundred years to reach the near side of it and thirty thousand more to pass through.

So which answer is right? It depends on what you decide a solar system is made of. If it is planets, it ends at Neptune. If it is material, it ends somewhere out in the frozen ring. If it is the Sun's influence, it ends where the Sun stops pushing, or where the Sun stops pulling, and those are two very different fences. The honest reply is that the solar system does not have an edge so much as a fade.

6.title: Eight Worlds Around One Star
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ceres was called a planet from 1801 to about 1850
Pluto was the ninth planet from 1930 to 2006
Eris, found in 2005, is more massive than Pluto
The IAU planet test has three parts
Pluto passes two of them and fails the third
Dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake

blocks.prompt: What Counts as a Planet
blocks.text:
On the first day of the nineteenth century, a Sicilian astronomer named Giuseppe Piazzi found a faint point of light creeping against the stars in the gap between Mars and Jupiter. He had discovered Ceres, and for about fifty years the textbooks listed it as a planet. Then astronomers aimed better telescopes at the same gap and found Pallas, then Juno, then Vesta, then dozens more, and eventually thousands. Ceres had not changed. What changed was the company it kept. A single body between Mars and Jupiter is a planet. One of thousands is an asteroid. Ceres was quietly reclassified, and almost nobody minded.

The same story ran again a century later, and this time people minded very much.

Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930, and Pluto took its place as the ninth planet. It was an awkward fit from the start. Its orbit is tilted seventeen degrees out of the flat plane the other eight share, and it is stretched enough that for twenty years of every 248 year lap, Pluto rides closer to the Sun than Neptune does. Estimates of its size kept shrinking as measurements improved. By the 1990s astronomers were finding other frozen bodies out past Neptune, in a wide band now called the Kuiper Belt, and Pluto started to look less like a lonely ninth world and more like the brightest member of a crowd. In 2005 a team led by Mike Brown found Eris, which turned out to be more massive than Pluto. The choice became unavoidable: admit Eris, and whatever came next, or draw a line.

In 2006 the International Astronomical Union drew the line. A planet, it declared, must do three things: orbit the Sun, be massive enough that its own gravity pulls it round, and clear the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto passes the first two and fails the third. It shares its lane with countless frozen siblings and does not govern them. Pluto became a dwarf planet, alongside Ceres, Eris, Haumea, and Makemake, and the count of planets fell to eight.

The decision still annoys people, and some of the objections are good ones. The third rule describes a body's surroundings rather than the body itself, so the same object could qualify in one orbit and fail in another. Drop Earth into Pluto's orbit and Earth would not clear it either. Planetary scientists who study these worlds up close point out that Pluto has mountains of water ice, a nitrogen glacier roughly the size of Texas, a thin blue haze of atmosphere, and five moons, which makes it a strange thing to call not a planet.

But that objection misses what the rule was built for. The eight are not a random sample of round things. Each one dominates its region, having spent four billion years absorbing or flinging away everything that came near it. Pluto belongs to a different population entirely, one with hundreds of known members and probably far more. Filing it next to Jupiter hides that fact instead of revealing it.

Here is the part worth keeping. Nothing happened to Pluto in 2006. It did not shrink, wobble, or move. Only the paperwork changed. Nature does not sort itself into categories; we do that, because sorting is how we notice patterns. Ceres taught astronomers that the asteroid belt existed. Pluto taught them that the Kuiper Belt existed. In both cases the demotion was not a punishment. It was the moment we worked out that a thing we thought stood alone had a whole family standing behind it.
